[MUJAHID:v1p73#2/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | holds | Adam was taught the names of everything God created; the angels were asked to identify the things shown to Adam.
[MUQATIL:2:31/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | God taught Adam the names of every terrestrial animal and bird, naming creatures such as horses, mules, and donkeys individually.
[MUQATIL:2:31/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | God displayed the named creatures to the angels on earth and challenged them to identify them if truthful about the coming corruption and bloodshed.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yūnus reports that names for letters and other invariable words vary in grammatical gender: some Arabs treat them as feminine and others as masculine.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Some Arabs pronounce Law as Lawʾ, analogous to al-naʾūr, to avoid the excessive loss that inflection would cause to a wāw preceded by fatḥ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The names Hū and Hī double their final wāw or yāʾ when used as names, since those endings are not ordinary inflectional endings.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl analyzes Dhū as having the basic pattern faʿl with fatḥ on dhāl, supported by its forms Dhawā and Dhawū.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Kay and Fī lengthen their final yāʾ because Arabic has no ordinary word ending in yāʾ preceded by fatḥ; Fī would also be too reduced if nunated.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Lā and Fī are extended in both declinable and diptote naming, masculine and feminine, to prevent names from collapsing to one letter in connected speech.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When Dhā or Mā becomes a name, it is lengthened; as a feminine name it is diptote because the original forms are masculine.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Fū is replaced by Famm when isolated because Arabs already changed its final wāw to mīm to fit a familiar noun pattern; otherwise it would be derived from Fūh.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Letter names such as Bāʾ, Tāʾ, and Fāʾ are lengthened when made names; as names for words they remain indefinite, as shown by their accepting the article.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Alphabet names used for words resemble indefinite Ibn Makhāḍ and Ibn Labūn, unlike fixed definite species names such as Sām Abras and Umm Ḥubayn.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In spelling, alphabet letters are shortened and left unvowelled because they are pauses and sounds, not lexical names; Qāf, Ṣād, and Dāl show the pause form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الراجز | reports | The rajaz poet uses Kāf, Mīm, and Sīn with a masculine adjective, ṭāsima.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Pronouncing spelled letters is like making sounds and stopping, unlike wāḥid ithnān, where wāḥid is a fully inflected noun.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | A trusted informant heard speakers transfer the hamza of arbaʿa onto the preceding hāʾ in thalātha arbaʿa; the hāʾ stays fixed like a consonant in connected speech.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl says spelled letter sequences retain their alphabet names, as in lām alif; a poetic line attests writing that sequence.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Zāy has two spelling pronunciations: one patterned like Kay, and the more common one Zāy, patterned like Wāw.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r24] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Particles such as Umm, Man, ʾIn, and Mudh do not change when named because they resemble short nouns such as Yad and Dam.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r25] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Naʿam and Biʾs remain unchanged because they are verbs; verbs are grammatically masculine and are not treated as ordinary names of words.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r26] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Any alphabet letter made a name for a letter, a word, or something else follows the naming pattern of Lā, as in Bāʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الراعي | reports | Al-Rāʿī uses Kāf and Mīm with a feminine verb, showing the alternative feminine agreement.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When these items are pronounced with a vowel in context, fatḥ is preferred because they behave like verbs such as kāna.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A letter name used for the letter itself is declinable; when it names a word, the form follows the gender language chosen by the speaker.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Turning a particle into a name requires changing its former grammatical state, just as naming from a verb changes it into a noun.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl distinguishes ʾan and ʾin: ʾan is noun-like and can represent a verbal noun, while ʾin is verb-like.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Law and ʾAw end in sukūn; when made names they follow Layt and ʾIn in gender and declension, but their final wāw is doubled.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالحروفوالكلمالتيتستعملوليستظروفاولاأسماءغير#545/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Abū Zubayd’s verse shows the named forms Laytā and Lawā with lengthened final consonants.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A masculine given a feminine name of four or more letters is diptote because the naming departs from the form originally suited to masculine referents, like a foreign name.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some feminine forms, including Yafʿa and Rabʿa, can describe either males or females, unlike forms restricted to feminine referents.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Feminine-only adjectives used of masculine names are understood as originally describing a thing, person, or eye.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Wind words such as Ḥarūr, Shimāl, Janūb, and Samūm are usually adjectives in Arab usage, so a man named by one is declinable.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Al-Aʿshā’s rīḥan dabūran line supports describing feminine rīḥ with the masculine-form word dabūr.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Wind words are rarely treated as nouns; the cited poetry supplies such noun-like examples, which are then indeclinable when used as men’s names.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Established feminine names such as Suʿād, Zaynab, and Jayʾal are diptote, while masculine nouns used as men’s names, such as Rabāb and Dalāl, are declinable.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Names such as Khurūq, Kilāb, and Jimāl are declinable because these forms can denote masculine groups and are not exclusive feminine names.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | ʿAnūq is declinable because its feminine ending is the masculine plural pattern; it differs from ʿAnāq, a feminine species name.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nisāʾ is declinable as a masculine name because it is the plural of Niswah, like other masculine-plural forms.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | ʿAnāq, ʿAqrab, ʿAqāb, and ʿAnkabūt exemplify feminine names that make a masculine bearer diptote.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A feminine collective with no singular, such as Ibil or Ghanam, is treated like a feminine singular and is diptote when used as a masculine name.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Dh irāʿ is declinable as a masculine name because it became common and established for men, and it can describe a masculine noun such as thawb.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The preferred treatment of Kurāʿ is diptote; declension by analogy with Dh irāʿ is attested but is the weaker analysis.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A man named Thumānī or Thalāth is diptote because each is a feminine numeral form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r6] SIBAWAY

H, d. 180 · author | holds | The diminutive Ḥubayr from Ḥubārā remains diptote because the original name is feminine even after the diminutive element is removed.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Masculine names from feminine adjectives such as Ḥāʾiḍ, Ṭāmiṯ, and Mutʾim are declinable because those forms are masculine in morphology while describing females.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl explains that faʿūl and mifʿāl lack feminine marking because they entered usage as masculine forms that can describe feminine referents.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميةالمذكربالمؤنث)#539/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Names such as Qāʿid, Ḍārib, and ʿĀqir remain declinable when intended as feminine descriptions, by analogy with masculine forms used for females.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايبينونحركتهوماقبلهمتحرك)#731/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A suffixed pronoun yāʾ, whether genitive or accusative, keeps its vowel because it is weak and hidden rather than a case ending.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايبينونحركتهوماقبلهمتحرك)#731/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Some speakers omit pause hāʾ from clipped mā forms, by analogy with ʾikhsha; ʾIn is not a parallel because nothing was deleted from it.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايبينونحركتهوماقبلهمتحرك)#731/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In majīʾ ma jiʾta and mithl ma anta, pause hāʾ is obligatory because majīʾ and mithl are independent nouns; unlike the clipped particles, the first element is a noun.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايبينونحركتهوماقبلهمتحرك)#731/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | A pause hāʾ may follow the weak alif in hāʾulāʾ and hahunā for clarity; it is avoided with inflected nouns such as afʿā and aʿmā, where it could be confused with possessive hāʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايبينونحركتهوماقبلهمتحرك)#731/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Hāʾ is not attached after a preceding sukūn; many Arabs also omit it in pause when the ending is clear from context.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايبينونحركتهوماقبلهمتحرك)#731/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Vocatives and lament forms add hāʾ after long alif, wāw, or yāʾ in pause to sustain and clarify the call, then drop it in connected speech.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايبينونحركتهوماقبلهمتحرك)#731/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Speakers who make the yāʾ quiescent do not add hāʾ in pause, since nothing has been deleted from the connected form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايبينونحركتهوماقبلهمتحرك)#731/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Some forms add hāʾ after Hī and Hū in pause because their final yāʾ and wāw are not inflectional endings and are not left fully quiescent.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايبينونحركتهوماقبلهمتحرك)#731/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The same pause hāʾ appears in forms such as khudh-hu bi-ḥukmika; speakers who omit it with the earlier pronouns omit it here too.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايبينونحركتهوماقبلهمتحرك)#731/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Hāʾ and alif can both clarify a weak ending in pause: ḥayhalā becomes ḥayhal bi-ʿAmr in connection, though ḥayhal may also remain.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايبينونحركتهوماقبلهمتحرك)#731/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Anā retains final alif in pause and has no hāʾ variant; its short, hidden nūn and status as a minimal independent word distinguish it from Hū.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايبينونحركتهوماقبلهمتحرك)#731/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | No pause hāʾ is added to a fully inflected ending such as aḥmar, whose final changes for case and accepts the article.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايبينونحركتهوماقبلهمتحرك)#731/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Verbs such as ẓanna and ḍaraba likewise take no pause hāʾ because their final consonants vary with inflection.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايبينونحركتهوماقبلهمتحرك)#731/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Interrogative particles clipped from mā, such as ʿalāma, fīma, lima, bima, and ḥattāma, preferably take hāʾ in pause because deletion leaves a weak ending.
[SIBAWAYH:الذيلميتعدهفعلهإلىمفعولوالمفعولالذيلميتعدإليهفعلفاعلو#16/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh frames the discussion around whether a verb's action extends to an object and whether that object receives an action from an agent.
[SIBAWAYH:الذيلميتعدهفعلهإلىمفعولوالمفعولالذيلميتعدإليهفعلفاعلو#16/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Active and passive participles, and verbal nouns, can work like a verb that governs one object.
[SIBAWAYH:الذيلميتعدهفعلهإلىمفعولوالمفعولالذيلميتعدإليهفعلفاعلو#16/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Adjectives and other word forms modeled on verbs may govern similarly, but they do not have the full strength of a verb or its participles.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكضربعبداللهزيدافعبداللهارتفعههناكماارتفعفيذهب#20/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In ضرب عبد الله زيدا, ʿAbd Allāh is the raised subject as in ذهب, while Zayd is the object governed by the transitive verb.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكضربعبداللهزيدافعبداللهارتفعههناكماارتفعفيذهب#20/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Spatial distances can be governed like spans of time: ذهبت فرسخين and سرت الميلين parallel ذهبت شهرين and سرت اليومين.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكضربعبداللهزيدافعبداللهارتفعههناكماارتفعفيذهب#20/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Temporal complements are stronger because verb forms encode past and future, whereas places have no corresponding verb forms derived from them.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكضربعبداللهزيدافعبداللهارتفعههناكماارتفعفيذهب#20/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Places resemble named entities and physical bodies, while time is the passage of night and day and thus closer to the verbal event.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكضربعبداللهزيدافعبداللهارتفعههناكماارتفعفيذهب#20/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The object may precede the subject without changing their roles; this is good, common Arabic, used to foreground what matters more to the speaker.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكضربعبداللهزيدافعبداللهارتفعههناكماارتفعفيذهب#20/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Even an intransitive verb governs its verbal noun because the verb identifies an event but does not specify its kind or manner.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكضربعبداللهزيدافعبداللهارتفعههناكماارتفعفيذهب#20/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Verbal nouns can specify intensity, manner, number, or a subtype of an event, as in قعدتين and قعد القرفصاء.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكضربعبداللهزيدافعبداللهارتفعههناكماارتفعفيذهب#20/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Verbs govern temporal expressions because their forms indicate whether an event occurred in past time or will occur in future time.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكضربعبداللهزيدافعبداللهارتفعههناكماارتفعفيذهب#20/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Temporal nouns may be treated as adverbs or left without that label; verbs can govern them broadly, as they govern event nouns.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكضربعبداللهزيدافعبداللهارتفعههناكماارتفعفيذهب#20/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Verbs also govern derived place nouns and locations, since an event entails a place even when the speaker does not name it.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكضربعبداللهزيدافعبداللهارتفعههناكماارتفعفيذهب#20/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | rejects | Sībawayh reports that some speakers say ذهبت الشام by analogy with an indefinite place, but calls this anomalous because ذهب does not select Syria specifically.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكضربعبداللهزيدافعبداللهارتفعههناكماارتفعفيذهب#20/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | He cites Saʿida ibn Juʾayya's verse about the fox following a path as poetic evidence in the discussion of verbs and spatial complements.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh distinguishes eight inflectional and fixed-ending categories, which collapse into four pairs in pronunciation: nasb/fatḥ, jarr/kasr, rafʿ/ḍamm, and jazm/pause.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | He illustrates fixed endings on non-declinable nouns with fatḥ, kasr, ḍamm, and pause examples such as حيث, أولاء, قبل, and من.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Past verbs have fatḥ; their verbal pattern resembles the imperfect, appears as an adjective, and can occupy a conditional clause.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Imperatives end in pause because they are neither used as adjectives nor occupy the imperfect's syntactic role.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Particles take fixed fatḥ, kasr, ḍamm, or pause, as in سوف وثم, the prefixed bāʾ and lām, منذ, and من وهل وبل وقد.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | No verb takes fixed ḍamm because the non-imperfect verb classes are only the past and command patterns.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The dual noun uses an uninflected long-vowel case ending: alif in rafʿ and yāʾ in jarr and nasb, distinguishing it from the sound plural.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The dual noun's second suffix is nūn with kasra, compensating for the loss of short-vowel inflection and tanwīn.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The sound masculine plural uses wāw with ḍamma for rafʿ, yāʾ with kasra for jarr and nasb, and an open nūn to distinguish it from the dual.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The feminine plural tāʾ takes kasra in jarr and nasb; Sībawayh analogizes its ending to wāw and yāʾ and its tanwīn-like suffix to nūn.

عوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The dual subject marker on imperfect verbs is alif plus nūn; the alif marks duality rather than serving as a case ending.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The four inflectional endings change under governing operators, while built endings remain fixed regardless of such operators.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The imperfect dual keeps nūn as its rafʿ marker, but nūn is not an inflectional ending because it is deleted in jazm.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The imperfect plural takes wāw with a preceding ḍamma and an open nūn, distinguishing plural from dual forms.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The second-person feminine singular imperfect uses yāʾ and an open nūn; the nūn drops in nasb and jazm.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The feminine plural imperfect adds nūn as a subject and plural marker and builds the verb on the singular ending, as in the past plural.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r24] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The nūn in يفعلن parallels the feminine plural past; its status as a pronoun and plural marker explains why it remains in forms like هل تفعلن.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r25] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Verbs are heavier than nouns because nouns are more basic and can stand without verbs, whereas a verb needs a noun to make an utterance.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r26] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Adjectival forms such as أبيض and أحمر resemble verbs in form, so they take fatḥ in the genitive as a heavier, diptote pattern.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r27] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An adjective is weak without a noun host, but works well after a noun; adjectives also resemble verbs in meaning and can govern an object.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r28] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Actual nouns such as أفكل and أكلب remain fully declinable in the indefinite because the verb-like pattern is adjectival only when used as a description.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r29] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Indefinites are lighter and more declinable than definites; definiteness is added later, so most forms decline while indefinite.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Rafʿ, jarr, nasb, and jazm are inflectional endings on declinable nouns and imperfect verbs, whose initial augment letters are hamza, tāʾ, yāʾ, or nūn.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r30] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Singulars are more basic and declinable than plurals; broken plurals on patterns such as مساجد and مفاتيح are diptote.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r31] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Masculine is lighter and more basic than feminine; tanwīn marks the more declinable, lighter forms, while its absence marks heavier ones.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r32] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Diptote nouns regain genitive when made definite with alif-lām or placed in annexation, since those constructions also apply to fully declinable nouns.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r33] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A weak-final imperfect whose ending is silent in rafʿ drops that letter in jazm to distinguish the jussive from the indicative.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nouns take rafʿ, jarr, and nasb but not jazm; their declinability and tanwīn mean losing tanwīn does not also remove the case vowel.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Imperfect verbs take rafʿ, nasb, and jazm, not jarr; jarr belongs to a noun complement, which imperfect verbs do not have.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The imperfect resembles an active participle in meaning and can take lām, sa-, or sawfa in ways analogous to nominal markers.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Despite that semantic resemblance, imperfect verbs are not nouns because they cannot be substituted into noun positions.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In the Quranic example from 16:124, the lām in ليحكم yields a meaning comparable to لحاكم, like a nominal predicate. | mentions 16:124
[SIBAWAYH:وهيتجريعلىثمانيمجارعلىالنصبوالجروالرفعوالجزموالفتحوالضم#4/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Fixed endings belong to non-declinable nouns, verbs outside the imperfect pattern, and particles, which are neither nouns nor verbs.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Species epithets such as Abū al-Ḥārith and Thaʿāla are conventional proper forms shared by every member of a kind, unlike an individual proper name.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | One analysis makes muqbil a direct predicate, as in hādhā Zaydun muqbil; the other treats the following description as indefinite and the compound as attached to an indefinite phrase.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The second analysis is needed because an indefinite noun cannot be annexed to a definite one; the phrase is instead made indefinite.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ibn Labūn and Ibn Makhāḍ are indefinite because they accept the definite article.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh cites Jarīr’s Ibn al-Labūn, Abū ʿAṭāʾ’s Banāt al-Māʾ, and al-Razdaq’s Ibn al-Makhāḍ as article-bearing forms, showing these compounds are indefinite without the article.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Dhū al-Rumma’s articleless Ibn Māʾ example shows that removing the article leaves the phrase indefinite.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · ناس | rejects | Some claim every Ibn Afʿal compound is definite because it is indeclinable; Sībawayh rejects this, since Afʿal adjectives can be indefinite and indeclinable.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh adduces Dhū al-Rumma’s awlād aḥqab as a poetic example of an indefinite Afʿal form.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Pointing to Abū al-Ḥārith or Thaʿāla identifies a lion or fox as a kind, not one previously identified animal.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A name such as Zayd singles out an individual already known by distinguishing features or a defining report.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The common noun rajul can mean a particular whole man or any male human; Zayd removes that ambiguity by naming one individual.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Wild animals did not need individual names because they were not continuously present or recognizable by retained appearance; people individually named horses, camels, sheep, and dogs kept among them.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Names for particular species and subtypes, including Ibn Qitra and Banāt Awbar, function as definite labels for a recognized kind, unlike generic animal nouns that can be definite or indefinite.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abū ʿAmr treats compounds such as Ibn ʿArs as definite because an article cannot be added to their second element; Yūnus transmitted his view.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For Ibn Qitra and Ḥimār Qubbān, the lack of declension in the element after the first compound element also signals definiteness.
[SIBAWAYH:يكونفيهالاسمالخاصشائعافيالأمة|ليسواحدمنهاأولىبهمنالآخر#243/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بعض العرب | reports | Some Arabs say hādhā Ibn ʿArs muqbil with muqbil nominative; Sībawayh gives two possible grammatical analyses.

[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p158/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | rejects | Jurjānī refines that account: alladhī introduces a clause already known as a story, distinguishing a particular person from others for the hearer.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p158/r4] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Even when the relative clause gives new information about the person, its event must already be known in general; the hearer learns which person it describes.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p320/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Metaphor is not a transfer of a word's name but a claim to its meaning: calling a man a lion implies courage, understood by inference as in metonymy.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p391/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Individual words were established to be joined so that benefits arise between them, not simply to disclose their meanings in isolation.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p391/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Language conventions presuppose something already known: a name or pointing gesture identifies a known thing among others rather than creating knowledge of its referent.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p391/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | A proposition becomes intelligible through a composed sentence, either verb with noun or noun with noun; the relation of an event to its subject is not itself a lexical meaning.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p391/r4] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The challenge to name “these” assumes the angels can already identify the beings indicated, illustrating that names point to known referents.

[JISHUMI:v1p315#2/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو جعفر ونافع برواية ورش وابن كثير برواية القواس ويعقوب | reports | For two same-vowel hamzas across words, these readers pronounce the first and soften the second, indicating its vowel.
[JISHUMI:v1p315#2/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو عمرو وابن كثير برواية البزي | reports | When two across-word hamzas have matching vowels, these readers pronounce one and omit the other.

[JISHUMI:v1p315#2/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن عامر وحمزة وعاصم والكسائي | reports | These readers pronounce both hamzas, whether the two across-word hamzas have matching vowels or differ.
[JISHUMI:v1p315#2/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The softened or deleted hamza eases pronunciation, while retaining the hamza follows the original form.
[JISHUMI:v1p315#2/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Ādam can mean brownish hue in people, whiteness in gazelles and camels, and the earth’s face; adama also means duskiness.
[JISHUMI:v1p315#2/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | One etymology derives Ādam from the earth’s surface; on this derivation the name is declinable when indefinite.
[JISHUMI:v1p317/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الزجاج | reports | ʿArḍ originally means a side or region; width is named as the opposite of length, and presenting goods displays their sides.
[JISHUMI:v1p317/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قتادة وغيره | reports | God taught Adam the meanings of names, since names without meanings convey nothing.
[JISHUMI:v1p317/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن عباس ومجاهد وأكثر المفسرين | reports | The comprehensive teaching included crafts, tools, cultivation, foods, medicines, mining, trees, fruits and their uses, and what serves religion and worldly life.
[JISHUMI:v1p317/r12] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الربيع | reports | An alternative says Adam was taught the names of the angels.
[JISHUMI:v1p317/r13] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن زيد | reports | Another alternative says Adam was taught the names of his descendants.
[JISHUMI:v1p317/r14] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | prefers | The comprehensive interpretation is stronger because the wording says all names, and most scholars hold it.
[JISHUMI:v1p317/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | To turn away is to withdraw; a person’s ʿarḍ was variously glossed as what earns praise or blame, good character, or lineage.
[JISHUMI:v1p317/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · علي بن عيسى | reports | ʿArḍ is the aspect of a person that he protects from harm and disgrace.
[JISHUMI:v1p317/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The root sense of ʿarḍ is appearance: width makes an object visible, presentation displays it, and an ʿaraḍ is an accident that alters a body’s quality.
[JISHUMI:v1p317/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Inbāʾ means informing; nabaʾ is news, and some restrict the word to news of great importance.
[JISHUMI:v1p317/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | Some say nabaʾ is used only for news of momentous significance.
[JISHUMI:v1p317/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن عباس | reports | The pronoun in ʿaraḍahum refers to created beings that God showed Adam; Ibn ʿAbbās summarizes this as displaying creation.
[JISHUMI:v1p317/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · مجاهد | reports | Another grammatical account supplies “owners of the names”; nonrational beings take the plural masculine by predominance.
[JISHUMI:v1p317/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | rejects | The suggestion that the pronoun refers to the names themselves is invalid because names as abstractions cannot be presented, and the wording does not fit presentation in heaven.

[JISHUMI:v1p318/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | God presented the beings after creating them; alternatively, He impressed their forms upon the angels’ hearts, and asked for the names and uses of the named things.
[JISHUMI:v1p318/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | One explanation says the angels had thought that a vicegerent from among themselves would avoid the corruption expected from Adam’s progeny and be better for them; the challenge exposed their ignorance of hidden realities.
[JISHUMI:v1p318/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | An alternative says Adam learned every language except the language in which God addressed him, which arose by convention.
[JISHUMI:v1p318/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | One account says God made Adam know the names by necessity; another says He taught him the angels’ language, through which Adam learned all languages.
[JISHUMI:v1p318/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | God taught names of individual beings by bringing each thing before Adam and teaching its name in every language, purpose, benefit, and harm; Adam did likewise for the angels.
[JISHUMI:v1p318/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | The angels knew some of the information because their commissioning preceded Adam’s.
[JISHUMI:v1p318/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | Another account distributes languages, useful knowledge, and crafts among angelic groups, who recognized Adam’s truth when he listed them all.
[JISHUMI:v1p318/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | The angels may instead have known because God informed them before creating Adam.
[JISHUMI:v1p318/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | Another account says a miracle established Adam’s truthfulness to the angels.
[JISHUMI:v1p318/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | This was Adam’s miracle because it exceeded ordinary experience; God perfected his intellect, commissioned him as a prophet, and made this his miracle.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p118/r15] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | reports | One etymology derives Ādam from adama, reddishness tending toward black; its plurals are udm and awādim, and it is indeclinable.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p118/r16] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قوم | reports | Another etymology derives Ādam from the surface of the earth, as if an angel formed it; this account gives plurals Ādamūn and awādim and requires declension.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p119/r13] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قوم | reports | Others say Adam learned names in every language spoken by his descendants.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p119/r14] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أبو علي الفارسي | rejects | Ibn Jinnī reports Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī’s extreme claim that Adam knew everything, even grammar as advanced as Sībawayh’s; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this wrong on several grounds.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p119/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from the Prophet says Ādam was created from all the earth’s soil, so his descendants vary in color, temperament, and moral character.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p119/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · جمهور الأمة | prefers | The majority of the community understand the names as labels for things; another group takes them to mean the persons themselves, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the first view because the verb “taught him” supports it.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p119/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن عباس وقتادة ومجاهد | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and Mujāhid say Adam learned the names of every created thing, small and great.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p119/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الطبري | prefers | Al-Ṭabarī says Adam learned the names of his descendants and the angels, preferring this because the next clause says God displayed “them” to the angels.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p120/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أكثر العلماء | reports | Most scholars say God taught Adam the uses of every thing and what is beneficial for it.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p120/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قوم | reports | Some infer that the command to inform the angels charges them with what they cannot do, showing that such a charge is permissible because God knew they lacked the knowledge.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p120/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The demonstrative “these” naturally indicates that visible persons were present when God displayed them to the angels.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p120/r14] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | prefers | Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s own reading is that God taught Adam names, displayed concrete kinds first to Adam and then to the angels, and asked the angels to name them before Adam did so.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p120/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | If the names meant all things, “displayed them” can mean presenting each community or kind; if they meant labels, Ubayy’s feminine reading fits.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p120/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The masculine plural “them” can refer to the objects because the word “names” can signify the objects named.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p120/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Anbiʾūnī means “inform me”; nabaʾ means news, and the word nabīʾ derives from it.

[TABRISI:2:31#3/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | A third account says God showed one example from each kind: failure to name an actual object leaves less excuse than failure to identify something from its description.
[TABRISI:2:31#3/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The display shows Adam better suited to stewardship and earth's cultivation because he could find crafts, farm, locate water, and extract minerals and deep-sea treasures through subtle knowledge.
[TABRISI:2:31#3/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | This supports the view that Adam learned the properties of things; if the angels could not identify visible things, they were even less able to know unseen matters.

[TABRISI:2:31/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Another derives Ādam from complexion or color; on this derivation the name remains indeclinable when indefinite.

[TABRISI:2:31/r16] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | In this context, inbāʾ, informing, and reporting are near-synonyms; nabaʾ means a report, and the verb can take two objects, or three by analogy with iʿlām.

[TABRISI:2:31/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو عمرو والبزي | reports | They use one hamza for two matching hamzas, leaving one of them unpronounced as a hamza.
[TABRISI:2:31/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · نافع برواية إسماعيل وابن كثير برواية ابن فليح | reports | They soften the first of two matching hamzas and pronounce the second fully.

[TABRISI:2:31/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Deletion and softening serve ease

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p62/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن زيد | reports | A fourth restricted interpretation says Adam learned the names of his descendants.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p30/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A word is anything uttered that conveys something by convention, a definition that includes both single words and compounds while excluding writing and gestures.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p30/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Words do not naturally or essentially signify their meanings, since their meanings vary across places and times whereas essential properties do not.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p30/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عباد | reports | ʿAbbād argues that without special correspondences between particular words and meanings, assigning each word to its meaning would privilege one possibility without a determinant.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p30/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Rāzī answers that this argument would also make the world's creation at one particular time, and each person's particular proper name, inexplicable as an ungrounded preference.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p30/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Some words happen to imitate their meanings: qaṭā and laqlaq imitate sounds, while khadm suits eating moist food and qadm eating dry food; Ibn Jinnī gives many such examples.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p30/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعضهم | reports | Some scholars assert that God stipulated the word-meaning assignments: human speech cannot establish its own first convention without an infinite regress, and they cite God's teaching Adam all the names. | mentions 2:31
[RAZI-FULL:v1p30/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Rāzī replies that people could establish word meanings by gesture, and that God's teaching Adam could mean inspiration or teaching languages coined by people before Adam. | mentions 2:31
[RAZI-FULL:v1p39/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | A proposed definition makes a noun a word that accepts inflection at its original formation; Rāzī rejects it because inflection is incidental and the definition's exclusions do not establish the noun's essence.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p39/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī defines a noun as what indicates a meaning in itself, without being joined to another meaning.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p39/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Rāzī argues that the pronoun in “in itself” makes the definition defective: if it refers to the signifier, the definition is circular or also fits particles and verbs; if to the signified, it yields an impossible or inadequate account.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p39/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | If “in itself” means that a referent does not subsist in something else, the definition wrongly excludes names of attributes and relations, whose referents do subsist in another.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p41/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Defining a verb by occurrence in a particular time invites regress, makes true statements about time's beginning or the world's primordial nonexistence false, and would make God's eternal existence temporal.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p41/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | The objection also says that calling God existent from eternity would imply that God is temporal, which is impossible.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p41/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Defective verbs challenge the definition: if they denote an event in time they should be complete verbs, and if they do not, they should not count as verbs.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p41/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Names of actions seem to denote time because they denote expressions that themselves indicate a particular time.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p41/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | The active participle seems time-specific because it indicates present or future, never past.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p41/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī answers that linguistic definition requires only conceiving a term's meaning, whether true or false; the first objections do not invalidate the definition on that basis.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p41/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī treats kāna as complete in every use: it means occurrence, either of an independent entity or of one thing's being described by another.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p41/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | In a construction such as “Zayd was standing,” kāna still means occurrence, but the occurrence is the relation of Zayd being described as standing, which requires naming both relata.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p41/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A word counts as a verb by indicating time directly, not through an intermediary; Rāzī denies that the active participle's temporal range is limited as alleged.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p153/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī treats the challenge to name the things as evidence that the angels' preceding claim was false, while presenting the inference as a question.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p153/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | He takes 2:33 to show that the angels had not known this before the episode and had doubted God's knowledge of all things. | mentions 2:33
[RAZI-FULL:v2p153/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Revelation of the corruption forecast is unlikely because repeating an inspired fact would be pointless; he infers conjecture, forbidden by 17:36 and 10:36. | mentions 17:36, 10:36
[RAZI-FULL:v2p153/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās reports that God addressed the angels who had been Iblīs's troops in the war against the jinn; their question about a corrupting successor drew God's anger, and they repented by admitting their ignorance.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p153/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الجن وقتادة | reports | A report attributed to the jinn and Qatāda says the angels privately expected every new creature to be inferior to them; Adam's knowledge exposed that boast, so they repented and confessed ignorance.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p153/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Some narrations add that God sent fire to burn the angels after they asked whether He would place a corruptor on earth.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p153/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · من تمسكوا بقصة هاروت وماروت | reports | The account says Hārūt and Mārūt condemned human sins and prayed against people; God warned that human desires would make them disobey, but they claimed they would resist and were sent down for a test.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p153/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · من تمسكوا بقصة هاروت وماروت | reports | In the story, Venus and her accompanying angel take human forms; the angels visit Venus, refuse sex unless they drink wine, then succumb to desire, and she imposes another condition.

item.text: The early notes cover the scope of Adam’s knowledge, what was displayed, and the angels’ challenge. They also include extended discussions of names and language, so those will need their own questions in the map.

[BURSEVI:v1p78#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · كشف الكنوز | reports | Kashf al-kunuz reports broad scholarly agreement that all names were divinely taught: God created in Adam necessary knowledge of words and the meanings they denote.

[BURSEVI:v1p78#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · بعض المفسرين | reports | Some exegetes say Adam learned a thousand trades and taught his children to seek worldly livelihood through crafts rather than religion; they list Adam as farmer, Noah as carpenter, Idris as tailor, Salih as merchant, David as armorer, Solomon as basket maker, and several prophets as shepherds.
[BURSEVI:v1p78#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · حديث | reports | A report says the best men's work is tailoring and the best women's work is spinning; the text also says Muhammad did much of the household tailoring.
[BURSEVI:v1p78#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The comprehensive wording includes names of creatures and names of God; if knowledge of creaturely names warrants the angels' prostration, knowledge of God's names warrants it even more.
[BURSEVI:v1p78#2/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The masculine plural pronoun in the account of displaying the names is used because rational beings occur among the named things and take grammatical precedence.
[BURSEVI:v1p78#2/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | To display something is to show it to another so that the viewer can recognize its condition.
[BURSEVI:v1p79/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · حديث | reports | A report says God displayed the named beings in forms as small as particles of dust.
[BURSEVI:v1p79/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Possibly God displayed one representative from each kind so the angels could learn the states and rules of the rest from it.
[BURSEVI:v1p79/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Teaching and displaying the names honored and elected Adam, disclosed hidden knowledge through a chosen servant, prevented angels and others from claiming superior knowledge, and manifested God's encompassing mercy.
[BURSEVI:v1p79/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The command to inform God was meant to rebuke and disable the angels, not to obtain an answer; such an impossible command can expose incapacity, as with image makers told to revive their creations on Judgment Day.
[BURSEVI:v1p79/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The challenge asks for the names of the existing beings and tests the angels' claim that they deserved vicegerency more than God's chosen appointee.
[BURSEVI:v1p79/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The verse shows that, after knowledge of divine unity, learning language is among the most valuable sciences, since God demonstrated Adam's superiority through it.
[BURSEVI:v1p79/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Anyone claiming superiority must supply evidence: the angels were asked for proof, and their speculation about unseen corruption was answered by their ignorance of names of what they could actually see.
[BURSEVI:v1p79/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The passage rebukes claimants and knowers alike: if people cannot name what they see, they should not presume to judge what they cannot see; knowledge should lead to love, and love to obedience.
[BURSEVI:v1p79/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · أبو بكر الواسطي | reports | Al-Wasiti says knowing God necessarily leads to loving Him, love to remembering Him, remembrance to tasting its sweetness, and that sweetness makes one turn away from other things.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p223/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The teaching clause coordinates with God’s prior speech and confirms its content; the opening of the teaching account suggests the dialogue followed Adam’s creation and occurred in his presence after the spirit was breathed into him. | mentions 2:30
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p223/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الجوهري | reports | Al-Jawhari argues that hamza has no known original position in this pattern, so the name’s plural and diminutive instead favor wāw; others do not accept his argument.

[ALUSI-FULL:v1p223/r13] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The plural asmāʾ is etymologically a sign for a thing, raising it into the mind through words assigned in any language, along with qualities and actions.

[ALUSI-FULL:v1p223/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | An alternative parses the teaching as coordinated with an omitted verb: God created Adam and taught him, created, fashioned and breathed into him before teaching him, or appointed him a vicegerent and taught him. | mentions 2:30

[ALUSI-FULL:v1p224/r22] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | The author rejects identifying the displayed items with the names themselves: the angels are asked for the names of those items, whereas asking about the items themselves would have said tell Me these.
